newsitem.title: USA: Martian dust storm menaces Pathfinder landing site.
newsitem.headline: Martian dust storm menaces Pathfinder landing site.

text.p: An unexpected, large dust storm on Mars is moving toward the July 4 landing site of NASA's unmanned Pathfinder spacecraft, researchers studying Hubble Space Telescope images said on Tuesday.

The dust storm is filling the Valles Marineris canyon system, a series of three-to-five-mile-deep (five-to-eight-km-deep) canyons stretching for 1,800 miles (3,000 km) and coming to within about 600 miles (970 km) of the Pathfinder landing site, according to a statement by the University of Colorado.

Unless the dust storm evolves into a massive, global event, its effects on the Pathfinder mission should be minimal, said Steve Lee of Laboratory for Atmospheric and Space Physics of the University of Colorado at Boulder.

"This is something we did not expect to see -- it's very early in the Martian year for major dust storms to occur," Lee said. "It could go away tomorrow, stay for weeks or turn into a global dust storm. We haven't seen a storm like this one before, so we just don't know."

The researchers took high-resolution colour images of the side of Mars where the landing site is located in the early morning, midmorning and early afternoon of June 27 to check weather conditions before the Pathfinder landing.

Hubble Space Telescope images and microwave observations taken by the researchers earlier this year indicated the planet was cold and cloudy, in stark contrast to the relatively warm and dusty conditions there when unmanned NASA spacecraft visited in the 1970s.
The Pathfinder, which consists of a stationary lander and a tricycle-sized surface rover known as Sojourner, will send images from Mars back to Earth beginnng on July 4.
The lander will touch down in an ancient flood plain known as Ares Vallis, about 500 miles (800 km) southeast of where the Viking 1 spacecraft landed in 1976.
In May NASA scientists said they believed Pathfinder would land on the Red Planent during a period of transition between the cold, cloudy period and that of dust storms.
But the newest images, taken last week, showed a dust storm in progress.
The team of researchers will continue to monitor Mars with Hubble for several months after the landing.
